newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US Nov industrial production to show gain.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US Nov industrial production to show gain.

text.p: U.S. industrial production strengthened in November after declining in October, spurred by inventory building, especially in the auto sector, economists said.

"We expect industrial production to be up 0.5 percent or 0.6 percent after a pretty sharp October drop of 0.5 percent," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
Feinman said "the big swing factor" for the industrial production data in November was auto production.
Auto production was down sharply in October due to the effects of a strike against General Motors by Canadian autoworkers.
After the strike was settled, production rebounded.

"There's been a rebound in auto and truck assemblies after a sharp decline due to the strike against GM in Canada and some weaker production by Ford and Chrysler, as well," said Sally Kleinman, vice president and senior domestic economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Kleinman is forecasting a 0.6 percent rise in November industrial production.

Besides the jump in manufacturing production, which accounts for about 85 percent of the industrial production figure, Kleinman sees a jump in utility output and an offsetting decline in mining production.

Mining accounts for less than seven percent of the total output measured by the Federal Reserve's industrial production report. Utility output accounts for a little less than eight percent, said Kleinman.
The higher utility output could be related to winter weather. It is also partly due to busier manufacturing activity.
"When manufacturing plants are running, they need power," said Kleinman.
Ram Bhagavatula, chief economist at Citicorp Global Finance, looks for a slightly more tempered industrial production rise of 0.4 percent for November.
"Some inventory building is going on in the economy so that's putting some upward presure on production," he said.
The financial markets need not be concerned about this level of industrial production because it contains no inflation threat, the economists said.
They look for the portion of the nation's mines, utilities and factories employed in the month's industrial output to rise to about 83 percent from 82.7 percent in October.

"That's still below where we were running in September when it was 83.4 and we're not back to the levels that would probably put upward pressure on commodity prices -- which would be between 84 and 85," said Kleinman.

"After smoothing out the gyrations, you see a manufacturing sector that's advancing at only a fairly moderate rate," said Feinman. "Consequently, it is not putting increasing strains on production or, ultimately, prices."
"We're so far from any inflation thresholds ... there's no concern about that," said Bhagavatula.
